lines.text: Add one real addition to last topic's page: a slot array, where each slot holds a physical offset and a length, and a record's own identity is that slot's own index, never its offset.
Delete a record sitting in the middle of the page, and compact it, physically closing the gap that deletion left behind.
Does that record's own identity survive being physically moved?
Yes, it does.
Its slot index stays exactly the same, even though its physical offset changes underneath it.
Run it for real: insert several records of different lengths into the page, and every one of them reads back correctly through its own slot index.
Delete the middle one and compact the page, and the surviving records' own physical offsets genuinely change.
Look closely at those same two surviving records.
Did compacting the page change their own slot indices at all?
No, neither one changed.
Each record's own slot index stayed exactly what it was before the deletion.
Run it for real: after compaction, the surviving records' own physical offsets had changed, but their own slot indices had not moved at all.
Now read each surviving record back, by that same slot index, after the compaction that physically moved it.
Does it still return the exact same content it held before the move?
Yes, exactly the same content.
The slot index was never tied to the old physical offset in the first place.
Run it for real: reading by slot index after compaction returned the exact same content as before, for every surviving record, byte for byte.

lines.text: Now try to insert one more record, one too large to fit in whatever free space is left on the page.
What happens?
The insert is rejected cleanly.
Every record already on the page stays exactly as it was.
Run it for real: the oversized insert was rejected cleanly, and every record already on the page, read back by its own slot index, was still exactly intact.
The documentation this page design is modeled on makes a stronger claim still: because a page's own size is fixed, a value too large to fit can't just spill onto the next page.
It has to be compressed, or broken up and stored somewhere else entirely. That's the real reason a whole separate storage mechanism exists for oversized values.
So, pulling this topic together: giving a record a name that never changes, separate from wherever it happens to physically sit, is the entire reason this indirection exists.
Move the bytes during compaction all you like; the name never has to be told.
And when something simply can't fit, the right answer is a clean rejection, not a corrupted page, which is exactly why oversized values end up living somewhere else altogether.
